reagents.name: Hydrochloric acid, 1.00 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of concentrated hydrochloric acid (6 M to 12 M), from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314+H318: Causes severe skin and eye burns and damage
H332+H302: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value: The acid on this bench is 1 mol/L, which is about 3.6% hydrogen chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's sheet for hydrochloric acid solutions of 0.1 M to 2.4 M, which covers this strength, gives the signal word Danger and three statements: under H314, that the solution burns the skin severely and damages the eyes; under H335, that it may irritate the airways; and under H303, that it may be harmful if swallowed. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and for working in a fume hood or a well-ventilated room. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up, and that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. After a splash on the skin, it says, the wet clothing is to come off at once and the skin be rinsed with water.

reagents.name: Sodium hydroxide solution, 1.00 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium hydroxide, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value: The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L, which is about 4% sodium hydroxide by mass (worked out from the molarity, not read from a source). The same supplier's sheet for sodium hydroxide solutions of 0.3 M to 6.0 M, which covers this strength, gives the signal word Danger and one statement, under the code H314: the solution burns the skin severely and damages the eyes. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and says that the mist, the vapour or the spray of the solution is not to be breathed. It says that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up. After a splash on the skin or the hair, it says, the wet clothing is to come off at once and the skin be rinsed with water.

reagents.name: Ammonium nitrate
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid ammonium nitrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed

note.value:
The ammonium nitrate on this bench is about 4 g of the solid, dissolved in 50.0 mL of water to a solution of about 1 mol/L. The supplier's sheet for the solid keeps it from heat, anything that burns, strong acids and powdered metals; it is not ground, and its dust is not breathed. Its sheet for the solution, which takes in this strength, prints no signal word and no hazard statement. Both call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: NOAA's record marks it as explosive as well as a strong oxidising agent, and says that clothing it gets on can be a fire risk once dry; a second supplier's sheet has such clothing taken off and washed, and asks, for the eyes, flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Aluminium

specificHeat.working: 24.35 J/(mol·K) ÷ 26.982 g/mol = 0.902453 J/(g·K), stored to three significant figures as 0.902 J/(g·°C). A kelvin and a degree Celsius are steps of the same size.

reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of aluminium metal, the solid and not its powder or dust, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The aluminium on this bench is a solid piece of about 50 g, heated in boiling water; it is not a powder. The supplier's sheet for aluminium prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It says that the dust burns, that fine powder and dust give off heat with water, and that acids set hydrogen free. It calls for eye and face protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for aluminium shot adds strong alkalis to the acids, so the piece is kept from this lab's acid and alkali. It lists water too, and too much heat, and says of water that it is the molten metal that reacts; here the piece goes into boiling water on purpose, as the experiment. For the eyes it asks flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once. NOAA's record marks the powder as reacting with water and apt to catch fire in air: the powder is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Iron

specificHeat.working: 25.10 J/(mol·K) ÷ 55.845 g/mol = 0.449458 J/(g·K), stored to three significant figures as 0.449 J/(g·°C). A kelvin and a degree Celsius are steps of the same size.

reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of iron metal, in bulk pieces, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The iron on this bench is a solid piece of about 50 g, heated in boiling water; it is not filings or powder. The supplier's sheet for iron in bulk pieces prints no signal word and no hazard statement. It lists acids and moisture among what the metal is kept from; here the piece goes into boiling water on purpose, as the experiment. It names nothing to be worn: it says to keep the metal from the eyes and to wash the hands.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a metal maker's sheet for iron as rod, shot and pieces asks for safety glasses and, for the eyes, flushing with water for 15 minutes or more; two suppliers' sheets for filings add gloves, protective clothing and a doctor, one of them at once. One classes fine filings as a flammable solid, and NOAA's record marks the powder as apt to catch fire in air: filings and powder are another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Zinc

specificHeat.working: 25.40 J/(mol·K) ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.388498 J/(g·K), stored to three significant figures as 0.388 J/(g·°C). A kelvin and a degree Celsius are steps of the same size.

appearance.value: white metal with a bluish-grey lustre

reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of zinc metal, as shot, sheet, foil or granules, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The zinc on this bench is a solid piece of about 50 g, heated in boiling water; it is not dust. The supplier's sheet for zinc as shot, sheet and foil prints no signal word and no hazard statement, puts the fire hazards with the dust and the powder, and keeps the metal from strong acids and strong bases. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for zinc shot adds water and too much heat, and says that hydrogen may come off where zinc meets water or damp air; here the piece goes into boiling water on purpose, as the experiment. It says that zinc may cause dermatitis and may rub the eyes sore; for the eyes it asks flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once. A third's calls zinc very toxic to water life: it is kept out of drains and waterways. By NOAA's record of the dust, another matter, zinc reacts violently with wetted ammonium nitrate: the two are kept apart.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Tin

specificHeat.working: 26.99 J/(mol·K) ÷ 118.71 g/mol = 0.227361 J/(g·K), stored to three significant figures as 0.227 J/(g·°C). A kelvin and a degree Celsius are steps of the same size.

reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of tin metal, as shot, granules, mossy pieces or foil, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:
The tin on this bench is a solid piece of about 50 g, heated in boiling water; it is not a powder. The supplier's sheet for tin as shot, granules, mossy pieces and foil prints no signal word and no hazard statement, and says that the finely divided metal may burn. It keeps the metal from halogens, sulfur, strong bases and strong oxidisers. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for tin shot adds acids, with which it says the metal gives off hydrogen, and a third's keeps tin from acids too: the piece is kept from this lab's acid. The second says that tin irritates the eyes, and NOAA's record adds the skin and the airways; for the eyes the second asks flushing with water for 15 minutes or more and a doctor at once. NOAA's record says that the powder, unlike the massive metal, corrodes in air: the powder is another matter.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

specificHeat.note: The specific heat of water at 25 °C and ordinary pressure, which the source prints as 4.1813 J/(g·K); the three-figure value is stored, the same figure as the aqueous reactions lab. It is used for the water in the cup and, as an idealisation, for every solution in it: for the mixed acid and base, and for the ammonium nitrate solution. How far a real solution of these strengths is from water was not read for this lab.

density.note: The density of water at 25 °C and ordinary pressure, which the source prints as 0.99705 g/mL; it is stored as 1.00 g/mL. It is used to turn the 50.0 mL of water into 50.0 g and, as an idealisation, to turn the 50.0 mL of each solution of part 1 into 50.0 g. The densities of the two solutions were not read for this lab.

note.value: The heat of mixing the two solutions as they are on the bench, worked out from the enthalpies of formation the table prints for each dissolved substance at a stated dilution. A litre of a 1.00 M solution holds one mole in about 55 moles of water, and the table has rows for one mole in 50 and in 75: the row for 50 is taken for the acid and for the base, and the row for 100 for the sodium chloride they make, which ends up in about twice as much water. Taking the nearest rows and not working between them moves the figure by about a tenth of one percent. The same figure is used whatever the run.

infiniteDilution.working: (−285.830) − 0 − (−229.994) = −55.836 kJ for each mole of water formed

notes.value: The stored figure for this part is −57.7 kJ for each mole of water formed: the heat given out when the acid and the base of this part are mixed at about this strength, worked out from a table of enthalpies of formation. The minus sign says that the reaction gives heat out. For solutions so dilute that more water would change nothing, the same table gives −55.8 kJ/mol. Any strong acid with any strong base gives close to the same figure, because the reaction is the same one each time: a hydrogen ion and a hydroxide ion make a molecule of water.

A careful run in this lab comes out a little under the stored figure, as a real cup does. Heat is already leaking to the room while the two solutions are still mixing, so the highest temperature the logger shows is a little below the one a cup with no leak would have reached. With the lid off or the stirrer still, the leak has more time or more room, and the result is lower again: that is why such a run does not count.

Two things are taken as simpler than they are. The mixed solution is given water's specific heat, and each millilitre of it is taken to weigh 1.00 g. And the cup, the lid, the stirrer and the probe are taken to absorb no heat at all. A careful bench deals with the second by finding the calorimeter constant, the heat the calorimeter itself takes up for each degree, and adding that heat in. It deals with the leak by reading on after the peak, drawing a line through the slow cooling, and carrying that line back to the moment of mixing: the temperature the line gives there is used in place of the peak.

enthalpy.working: (−341.155) − (−365.56) = +24.405 kJ for each mole of ammonium nitrate dissolved

note.value: The heat of dissolving the solid to a solution of about the strength made on the bench, worked out from the table's row for the crystal and its row for one mole in 50 moles of water. About 4 g in 50.0 g of water is one mole in 53 to 59 moles of water over the range of masses a run can have; the row for 50 is the nearest, and the next, for 75, is 0.5 kJ/mol higher. So the stored figure is within about one percent of the table's own for every run, and the same figure is used whatever the run. The table also prints rows for the ammonium ion and for the nitrate ion in water, −132.51 and −205.0. Their sum is not used: it is 2.36 kJ/mol above the table's own row for the dissolved salt, fully ionised, and that row agrees with the table's row for nitric acid where the row for the nitrate ion does not.

infiniteDilution.working: (−339.87) − (−365.56) = +25.690 kJ for each mole of ammonium nitrate dissolved

notes.value: The stored figure for this part is +24.4 kJ for each mole of ammonium nitrate: the heat taken in when a mole of the solid dissolves in about fifty moles of water, which is close to the strength made here, worked out from a table of enthalpies of formation. The plus sign says that dissolving takes heat in. The heat comes out of the water, which is why the cup gets cold. For a solution so dilute that more water would change nothing, the same table gives +25.7 kJ/mol, and an enthalpy of solution is usually quoted for that case.

The mass that cooled is the water and the salt together: once it has dissolved, the salt is part of the solution. A careful run in this lab comes out a little under the stored figure, as a real cup does. Heat is already leaking in from the room while the salt is still dissolving, so the lowest temperature the logger shows is not quite as low as a cup with no leak would have reached. With the lid off or the stirrer still, the leak has more time or more room, and the result is smaller again: that is why such a run does not count.

Two things are taken as simpler than they are. The solution is given water's specific heat. And the cup, the lid, the stirrer and the probe are taken to give up no heat of their own as they cool. A careful bench deals with the second by finding the calorimeter constant, the heat the calorimeter itself gives up or takes in for each degree, and adding that heat in. It deals with the leak by reading on after the lowest point, drawing a line through the slow warming, and carrying that line back to the moment the salt went in: the temperature the line gives there is used in place of the lowest point.

The specific heat of a metal is the heat that one gram of it takes in to warm by one degree, and gives out again as it cools by one. Each figure in the table of four is worked out from the heat capacity of a mole of the metal at 25 °C, as a table of thermodynamic values prints it, divided by the mass of a mole. The piece cooled from near 100 °C, and the lab uses the figure for 25 °C the whole way down: an idealisation, though for a solid metal at these temperatures the figure changes little.

A careful run in this lab comes out a little under the figure in the table, as a real cup does. Heat is already leaking to the room while the piece is still warming the water, so the highest temperature the logger shows is a little low. That makes the heat the water took in look smaller and the fall of the metal look larger, and both push the answer down. With the lid off or the stirrer still the answer is lower again, and may land nearer another metal: that is why such a run does not count.

Three things are taken as simpler than they are. The piece is taken to reach the cup at once, as hot as the bath; it is taken to arrive dry; and the cup, the lid, the stirrer and the probe are taken to absorb no heat. A careful bench heats the piece in a dry test tube that stands in the boiling water, so that no hot water comes with it, and tips it into the cup quickly. It finds the calorimeter constant, the heat the calorimeter itself takes up for each degree, and adds that heat in. And it reads on after the peak, draws a line through the slow cooling, and carries that line back to the moment the piece went in.

loggerStepSeconds.rationale: The logger takes one reading every 15 seconds: the lab's set-up. The engine counts steps of this length and reads no clock.

runOnSteps.rationale: One press of Run on lets 30 seconds pass, which is two readings: short enough that a careful run shows its peak and the turn after it in a few presses, long enough that the slow drift back shows.

loggerMaxSteps.rationale: The logger stops after an hour of readings. No run needs that long: with the stirrer still, the slowest curve turns back within nine minutes. The limit keeps a stored run small, and keeps a record edited by hand from holding the page up.

mixStirredPpm.rationale: Of the heat a change has still to give or take, the share given or taken in one 15-second step while the cup is stirred, in parts per million: 85%. A stirred cup is then within one part in a thousand of its end after a minute. The laboratory manual page read for the primer has its mixtures steady from about half a minute to a minute or two after mixing. Chosen with the next three so that a careful run lands within the tolerance at every seed.

mixStillPpm.rationale: The same share while the cup is not stirred: 15%, so that the change takes about five minutes to get most of the way. Slower than a real cup left alone is likely to be: it is made large enough that the heat lost to the room over that time puts an unstirred run outside the tolerance at every seed, as the titration lab makes each of its technique errors large enough to fail on its own. A real unstirred cup also reads unevenly, which the model leaves out.

lossLidOnPpm.rationale: Of the difference between the cup's temperature and the room's, the share lost in one 15-second step with the lid on, in parts per million: 0.5%, which is 2% a minute. A cup 7 °C above the room then cools by about a tenth of a degree a minute, so the drift back shows on the logger within a few presses, and a careful run reads between 0.4% and 3.1% low.

lossLidOffPpm.rationale: The same share with the lid off: 4%, eight times the share with it on. More than an open foam cup is likely to lose: it is made large enough that a run with the lid off is outside the tolerance at every seed.

startRangeTenths.rationale: The temperature the cup starts at, and the room with it, in tenths of a degree Celsius: 20.0 to 24.0 °C, a room. The solutions, the water and the cup have stood in the room, so before the change the logger draws a level line, and after it the cup drifts back towards the same temperature.

saltRangeCg.rationale: The mass of ammonium nitrate weighed out, in hundredths of a gram: 3.80 to 4.20 g, the specification's about 4 g, read on a balance that shows 0.01 g. About a twentieth of a mole, so the water cools by 5 to 6 °C.

metalRangeCg.rationale: The mass of the piece of metal, in hundredths of a gram: 48.00 to 52.00 g, the specification's about 50 g. In 50.0 g of water it gives a rise of about 4 °C for tin and about 14 °C for aluminium.

bathRangeTenths.rationale: The temperature of the boiling water the piece is heated in, in tenths of a degree Celsius: 99.0 to 100.0 °C. The page read for water gives 99.97 °C for its boiling point at one atmosphere; a bath is seldom exactly there, so the bath is read each time and not taken to be 100.

readingToleranceTenths.rationale: A temperature typed counts as the one the logger shows when it is within 0.1 °C of it, the edge included: the specification's rule. It lets a reading one step along a level stretch of the curve stand.

tolerancePercent.rationale: A run counts when its result is within 5% of the stored figure, the edge included. A careful run is between 0.4% and 3.1% low, from the heat the cup loses before the peak and from reading the temperature to 0.1 °C, which on the smallest rise, tin's 4 °C, is over 1% by itself. Each technique error alone puts a run 8% or more low. The tolerance sits between the two, and it is under half the gap between iron and zinc, the closest pair of the four metals, so a result within it is never nearer to the wrong metal.
